The improvement is particularly evident in high-delay and low-bandwidth environments.
author: Xuyang Liu, Zijian Zhang, Haibin Zhang, Jiamou Liu, Meng Li, Zhen Li, Mengmeng Zhou, Wei Shen, Peng Jiang, Cong Guo, Liehuang Zhu

title: High-Coverage Fault-Tolerant Cycle Construction for BCube Data Center Network
content: BCube, one of the representative server-centric data center networks, is of high practical value in high-performance computing clusters and large model distributed training. During the long-term operation of data centers, component failures have become commonplace, which easily lead to network partitions and service interruptions. Therefore, fault tolerance serves as the core foundation for guaranteeing service continuity and stable operation of data centers. Cycle structures are a critical topological foundation for network fault tolerance, as they provide redundant communication paths, enable deadlock-free parallel communication, and facilitate network load balancing. The capability of constructing valid cycles in faulty networks directly determines the resource utilization efficiency and service availability of data centers. In this work, we first develop a theoretical framework for cycle fault tolerance analysis in BCube and derive the exact value of its cyclic connectivity to evaluate the network’s capability to preserve cycles under node failures. On this basis, we propose a two-stage fault-tolerant cycle construction algorithm adapted to the structural characteristics of BCube. The first stage identifies the largest fault-free connected component containing cycles to define the effective region for cycle construction. In the second stage, multiple strategies are integrated to efficiently generate valid cycles within the component, while maximizing the coverage of available fault-free nodes. Experiments conducted on BCube networks of different scales under diverse fault scenarios verify that our algorithm achieves superior performance in terms of running efficiency and node coverage, as well as excellent scalability and fault robustness.
author: Baohua Niu, Hai Liu, Yan Wang, Baolei Cheng, Jianxi Fan

title: Differential Fault Attack on Atom: Bypassing the Double Key Filter Using Filtered Faults
content: In this paper, we present a Differential Fault Attack (DFA) on the lightweight stream cipher Atom, proposed by Banik et al. in IACR Transactions on Symmetric Cryptography (TOSC)-2021. It employs two key filters simultaneously during the pseudo-random generation algorithm phase, one of which depends on LFSR state bits. Due to this LFSR-dependent key filter, the authors claim that forming algebraic equations relating key and state bits as variables to the keystream bits is difficult unless the entire LFSR state is known. In contrast, we propose a method to formulate such algebraic equations without guessing any LFSR bits. This enables us to implement a successful DFA on Atom. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported DFA on Atom. In the proposed DFA, we identify the location of injected faults using a weighted ensemble of trained MLP and XGBoost models. To further improve accuracy, we filter out ML predictions with confidence below a predefined threshold. We found that this strategy significantly reduces the number of SAT solver invocations and improves the overall time complexity of the attack. Based on our experiments, we demonstrate a successful DFA on Atom within a practical time by injecting 18 faults, provided all are correctly identified. Obtaining a set of 18 correctly identified faults requires, on average, 52 fault injections. The attack requires a total of 70 keystream bits (normal and faulty combined) just after a fault injection and guessing two random key bits.
author: Vaibhav Dixit, Satyam Kumar, Santanu Sarkar

title: System-Level Isolation for Mixed-Criticality RISC-V SoCs: A “World” Reality Check
content: As RISC-V adoption accelerates, domains such as automotive, the Internet of Things (IoT), and industrial control are attracting growing attention. These domains are subject to stringent Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) constraints, which have driven a shift toward heterogeneous Systems-on-Chip (SoCs) integrating general-purpose CPUs, tightly coupled accelerators, and diverse I/O devices with different integrity levels. While such integration improves cost efficiency and performance, it introduces a fundamental safety and security challenge: enforcing system-level isolation in mixed-criticality environments. Although RISC-V International has proposed several hardware isolation primitives, including RISC-V Worlds, IOPMP, and SmMTT, their interoperability, scalability, and suitability for real-time systems remain insufficiently understood. In this paper, we present a comparative analysis of these primitives from the perspective of practical heterogeneous SoC designs. We implement an IOPMP, a World-based checker, and a modified RISC-V World checker that addresses key limitations of the baseline specification, and evaluate their trade-offs in terms of security guarantees and power–performance–area (PPA). Our results show that the World-based checker introduces a fixed, configuration-independent access latency, achieving lower worst-case delay than the evaluated alternatives while scaling predictably with system size. At the macro level, we estimate that the proposed modifications reduce SoC area by up to approximately 5% compared to a baseline design. All artifacts will be released as open source, and we expect these findings to directly contribute to the evolution and ratification of RISC-V specifications, as well as to the design of future RISC-V SoCs.
author: Luís Cunha, José Martins, Manuel Rodríguez, Tiago Gomes, Uwe Moslehner, Kai Dieffenbach, Glenn Farrall, Kajetan Nuernberger, Sandro Pinto, Thomas Roecker

title: Quantum at the Edge: Scalable Standalone FPGA Emulator for QAOA-Based Weighted-MaxCut
content: Quantum computing (QC) emulation is critical for exploring and advancing near-term quantum algorithms, given the ongoing scalability and reliability challenges of quantum hardware. While FPGA-based QC emulators have emerged as efficient alternatives to bridge the gap toward practical quantum computers, most existing solutions depend on high-performance systems, limiting their applicability in embedded and edge environments. In this work, we present a scalable, standalone FPGA-based emulator specialized for resource-constrained systems. Our design targets the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), particularly for the Weighted-MaxCut problem. By leveraging diagonal decomposition and a pipeline-centric hardware architecture, we reduce the computational complexity of QAOA from $\boldsymbol{O(N^{2})}$O(N2) to $\boldsymbol{O(N)}$O(N), where $\boldsymbol{N}$N $\boldsymbol{=}$= $\boldsymbol{2^{n}}$2n is the state dimension for $\boldsymbol{n}$n qubits. This reformulation and its architectural co-design significantly reduces hardware overhead, enabling larger qubit configurations on edge-level FPGAs. We encapsulate these optimizations into a hardware accelerator called the Quantum MaxCut Accelerator (QMA), which integrates seamlessly into a RISC-V platform, forming a self-contained emulator. Additionally, we introduce QC Emulator eXpress (QEX), a full-stack automation framework that streamlines QMA integration into configurable RISC-V platforms, significantly facilitating rapid and scalable emulator development and deployment. Through extensive prototyping of various QAOA emulators, our experiments confirm that the proposed QMA achieves energy reductions of up to $\textbf{907}\boldsymbol{\times}$907× compared to the CPU-only software baseline under the same standalone FPGA/RISC-V setting and reliably supports up to 9 qubits on a mid-tier FPGA. These results demonstrate the energy efficiency and scalability of the proposed system as a self-contained FPGA/RISC-V platform for edge-local QAOA emulation, prototyping, and HW/SW co-design exploration under resource-constrained conditions.
author: Seonghyun Choi, Kyeongwon Lee, Jae-Jin Lee, Woojoo Lee

title: ShBkDRL: Reliable Microservice Provision With Shared Backup in Dynamic Edge Computing
content: As a key 5G enabler, edge computing locates resources near users to enable low-latency services, and microservices architecture (MSA) decomposes monolithic services into microservices, easing deployment and scaling of mission-critical applications with high reliability requirements. Existing studies on microservice backup and deployment often adopt dedicated backup strategies, resulting in excessive redundancy and high resource consumption. This paper investigates reliable service deployment with shared backups in resource-constrained and dynamic edge environments, aiming to meet differentiated reliability requirements while optimizing resource efficiency. However, shared backups introduce interdependencies among services, complicating relationships among backup and deployment strategies, service reliability, resource costs, and loads. To model these intricate relationships, we divide microservices (service functions) of the same type into service function groups for sharing backups and formulate the problem as an integer nonlinear programming problem, proving its complexity. Moreover, the sequential arrival of requests in dynamic environments renders this problem a multi-stage decision problem, with high-dimensional resource constraints and a large-scale solution space adding complexity. Thus, we design a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based shared backup scheme with theoretical guarantees, which leverages DRL to capture long-term rewards and generate fractional solutions, while domain knowledge—specifically, the insight that providing additional backups to service function groups with low reliability yields greater reliability improvements—is used to adjust the fractional solutions. This adjustment helps prevent the DRL agent from falling into poor local optima and violating constraints. Finally, extensive experiments on real-world Alibaba traces show our method reduces costs by up to 70.52% compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
author: Yue Zeng, Junlong Zhou, Linhui Wang, Yong Xie, Baoliu Ye, Zhihao Qu, Pan Li, Song Guo

title: Scalable Stochastic Circuit Synthesis via Optimized Solution Space Exploration and Constrained Functional Transforms
content: Stochastic computing (SC) is an emerging computing paradigm known for its strong fault tolerance. To implement stochastic circuits with low hardware cost, state-of-the-art methods approximate a target function by a Bernstein polynomial and synthesize the corresponding circuit by properly assigning cubes, i.e., product terms, to realize the Bernstein polynomial. However, as the polynomial degree increases, cubes become larger and the solution space grows exponentially, rendering the existing methods impractical. To address this issue, we develop an optimized stochastic circuit synthesis method consisting of four key components: 1) an optimized method to quantize the coefficients of Bernstein polynomials for cube assignment, 2) an efficient solution space exploration method, 3) four acceleration techniques for solution space exploration, and 4) a constrained linear transformation technique that reduces the complexity of the function prior to synthesis. The experimental results show that compared to the state-of-the-art method, the proposed method reduces the area, delay, and area-delay product by $39.34\%$39.34%, $12.74\%$12.74%, and $45.09\%$45.09%, respectively. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates high scalability by being able to synthesize Bernstein polynomials of degrees up to 42, a value unreachable by prior methods.
author: Songchao Chen, Yi Jiang, Kuncai Zhong, Weikang Qian

title: PALIKV: PM-Resident Learned Index-Based Key-Value Store for the DRAM-PM-SSD Hierarchy
content: Persistent memory (PM) bridges the latency and cost gap between DRAM and SSDs. Within the DRAM–PM–SSD hierarchy, deploying key-value-separated key-value stores (KV-separated stores) is imperative for optimizing system longevity and performance. This architecture mitigates SSD write amplification and preserves PM endurance by minimizing writes. Existing KV-separated stores in the DRAM-SSD architecture, however, fail to fully exploit this three-tier hierarchy due to three issues. First, LSM-tree indexes incur high read amplification on PM. While learned indexes offer faster reads, they suffer from severe write-read asymmetry that can undermine overall efficiency in write-intensive workloads. Second, the lack of real-time obsolete data identification delays space reclamation. Third, contemporary KV stores treat PM as a passive write buffer, underutilizing its low read latency under skewed workloads. To address the above issues, we propose PALIKV – a PM-resident learned index-based KV store for the DRAM-PM-SSD hierarchy. We first design an adaptive two-level index that combines a PM learned index with a dynamic DRAM B+-tree buffer. This structure balances lookup efficiency with high write throughput while filtering redundant updates and extending PM lifespan. Second, the learned index enables real-time obsolete data identification. This facilitates an expedited garbage collection with device-specific reclamation granularity, thereby significantly reducing space amplification. Third, a hotness-aware data placement proactively migrates warm data from SSD to PM, allowing PM to serve skewed reads and eliminating the latency-constrained SSD from the critical read path. The experimental results unveil that PALIKV significantly outperforms SOTA KV-separated stores and DRAM-PM-SSD KV stores in terms of throughput and latency.
author: Hui Sun, Yajie Deng, Xiao Qin, Yi Zhou

title: Beyond Operator Patterns: Dependency-Centric Model Extraction From AOT-Compiled Deep Learning Binaries
content: Compiler-driven deployment has become a major source of model extraction risk in deep learning systems. Existing studies have shown that compiled binaries may still leak model structure and semantics, but most prior attacks implicitly focus on deployment regimes where graph structure remains relatively accessible. In contrast, the security implications of Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compiled models, which are increasingly important for resource-constrained edge deployment, remain underexplored. More importantly, AOT extraction is often formulated as a template-based abstract matching problem, while its primary difficulty lies elsewhere: compilation hides model semantics inside function–buffer interactions, memory reuse, and implicit execution dependencies. In this paper, we show that the significance of AOT model extraction lies not only in building a stronger attack, but also in revealing a more fundamental coupling between compilation and model recoverability. We argue that, in AOT binaries, the critical object that survives compilation is not merely an operator pattern, but the dependency structure shaped by compiler-managed execution and memory reuse. Based on this view, we propose ENNACE, a dependency-centric extraction framework that reconstructs hidden execution dependencies and then recovers fine-grained operator attributes from optimized AOT binaries. Extensive experiments show that our dependency-centric reformulation of AOT model extraction substantially strengthens attack capability, surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods, and offers practical guidance for both future attack design and defense development.
author: Minghui Li, Yang Li, Tongyu Wang, Liming Fang

title: Fast LM Head via Coarse-Fine Decomposition and Tile-Wise Weight Clustering
content: Large language models (LLMs) reuse each generated token as the next input during autoregressive decoding, making per-token latency a critical factor in practical inference performance. In this process, the LM Head performs a large-scale linear projection from the hidden state to the full vocabulary space at every decoding step, becoming one of the major bottlenecks in terms of memory bandwidth and latency. Existing output-layer approximation or vocabulary-pruning approaches can reduce the LM Head cost, but they may cause accuracy degradation due to logit-ranking distortion or task-dependent candidate omission. This paper reinterprets the LM Head as a candidate-screening problem and proposes a coarse-fine LM Head algorithm that restructures it into coarse and fine stages. The proposed method converts the LM Head weights into a compact codebook and an index map through tile-wise k-means clustering, and during online decoding, it computes full-vocabulary coarse scores using tile-wise LUTs and index streaming. Then, exact GEMV or GEMM using the original LM Head weights is performed only for the selected top-$k$k candidates. Experimental results show that the proposed method limits the average accuracy change to -0.21%p compared with the original LM Head across nine downstream benchmarks, while accelerating the LM Head computation by 5.82$\boldsymbol{\times}$× on average and up to 12.7$\times$×. In addition, end-to-end TPOT measurements demonstrate a speed-up of up to 1.18$\times$× on DGX Spark, and the method operates stably under various decoding lengths, batch sizes, and sampling conditions. The implementation and evaluation scripts are publicly available at https://github.com/HigherIdeal/CFHead.
author: Jung-Woo Kim, Seung-Hwan Yoon, Hye-Rin Lee, Hak-Bum Lee, Su-Min Oh, Seung-Yoon Kang, Young-Ho Seo

title: Leveraging the Error Margins of Approximate Adders for Fault Tolerance with Minimum Redundancy
content: Approximate Computing (AC) can be useful to applications with error resiliency, such as neural networks, to trade off between accuracy, performance, area, and power. Fault tolerance remains an open issue in AC since HW faults that are caused, for example, by radiation-induced effects, can lead to an arithmetic error out of application specification boundaries. Our approach guards approximate adders against HW faults by selectively inserting Hardware Error Detection (HED) redundancy, i.e., Double Modular Redundancy (DMR), only to the primitive adder cells of approximate adders that can cause an arithmetic error out of their resiliency boundaries (when corrupted by HW faults). Therefore, our approach introduces less area and delay overhead than hardening the whole circuit. We employ our methodology in various state-of-the-art approximate adders, such as low-latency and multi-bit approximate adders. We synthesize both the unhardened and hardened versions of the examined ASIC- and FPGA-based approximate adder architectures with Openlane and Vivado design flows, respectively. Our experimental results show that the proposed HED scheme can detect all out-of-boundaries errors: 1) without negating the original approximation gains of the unhardened design in terms of area and performance, and 2) by imposing significantly reduced overhead compared to the baseline (full DMR) hardened version.
author: Ioannis Tsounis, Dimitris Agiakatsikas, Mihalis Psarakis

title: Constructing Virtual FIFOs in CPU Cache Hierarchy for Software Data Plane Orchestration
content: Software Data Plane (SDP) has long been the foundation of IO performance in high-performance networking applications on general-purpose hardware. Modern networking scenarios often require line-rate deep networking application (DNAPP) capabilities for 100+Gbps network interfaces (NICs). In face of such challenges, current in-memory-hierarchy SDP data orchestration methods struggle to meet stringent throughput and latency requirements or minimize host interconnect congestion and cache resource contention. In this work, we formulate that, to ideally manage SDP’s packet receive queues (RXQs), a logical FIFO should be virtualized for each RXQ over the existing memory hierarchy. To this end, we propose FRM (FIFO-like RXQ Management), a holistic scheme for monitoring and managing RXQs within the cache hierarchy. FRM accomplishes FIFO virtualization through: (1) a dynamic allocation-prefetch framework that constructs a FIFO-like RXQ pipeline across middle-level caches, the last-level cache (LLC) and DRAM, and (2) an LLC apportionment framework that assigns LLC space for RXQs and prevents interference between them. Experiments show that FRM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art SDP-oriented prefetching methods. It improves peak throughput under random-sized packet loads by up to 60.7% and reduces near-saturation-load latency by 44.9% under IO-intensive benchmarks. Under heavy network loads, FRM reduces LLC writeback bandwidth by 41.2% and enhances cache performance for non-IO data access.
author: Zhiyuan Zhang, Jialin Liu, Zengshi Wang, Kanheng Jiang, Chao Fu, Jun Han

title: TFHEShield: Criticality-Aware Memory Reliability for TFHE
content: Torus Fully Homomorphic Encryption (TFHE) enables secure computation directly on encrypted data. However, TFHE incurs significant memory overhead, expanding data footprints by nearly three orders of magnitude compared to cleartext models. This massive volume of ciphertext must be stored in main memory, making it highly vulnerable to memory faults. Even a single fault in these ciphertexts can severely degrade inference accuracy, potentially causing the entire computation to fail. This critical vulnerability heightens the urgent need for reliable memory solutions tailored to TFHE-based inference systems, an area that remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present TFHEShield, a novel memory reliability architecture designed specifically for TFHE-based inference. Through a comprehensive fault-injection framework and theoretical analysis, we uncover that only a remarkably small fraction of ciphertext bits critically affects inference accuracy. Building upon this insight, TFHEShield integrates a fault-aware predictor that selects the critical-bit protection count for each TFHE ciphertext type according to offline fault-sensitivity profiling and real-time bit-error rates statistics. Additionally, we design a new memory architecture where the memory controller restricts error-correction operations to these critical segments, incurring negligible latency and minimal area overhead. Experiments on representative neural network workloads demonstrate that TFHEShield reduces protection area overhead by 81%-97%, lowers memory power consumption by up to 44%, and improves effective memory bandwidth by at least 10%, all while fully preserving inference accuracy.
author: Cheng Che, Jiangwei Zhang, Wen Sun, Shengyu Fan, Zhiwei Wang, Haoqi He, Dan Meng, Rui Hou

title: LIGHTeX: A Lightweight Framework for Extending Applications Into Trusted Execution
content: Many existing applications require strong security guarantees. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) have been proposed to address this need. However, running applications inside a TEE often requires substantial redevelopment to fit the constrained environment. Moreover, existing extension frameworks demand additional engineering effort to match specific logic models. To address these challenges, we present LIGHTeX, a lightweight frame-work that extends existing applications into Trusted Applications (TAs). Specifically, LIGHTeX enables this transition with minimal source code modifications. The extended TAs can run directly within the trusted runtime environment. LIGHTeX introduces a secure and efficient mechanism for system call reuse, reducing the development effort required to support system functions. Meanwhile, it reduces runtime overhead by optimizing context store/restore during world switching. These strategies enable LIGHTeX to operate effectively and significantly reduce runtime overhead incurred when extending applications to trusted executions due to environmental transitions. We prototype LIGHTeX and evaluate the performance on both single functions and real-world applications. The performance evaluation indicates that LIGHTeX requires only 1.67% code modification to successfully extend real-world applications into TAs. Performance tests indicate that LIGHTeX introduces an average overhead of only 11.73% for simple applications. Notably, in real-world application performance tests, the absence of interrupt preemption within the TEE leads to a maximum performance improvement of up to 60.25%.
author: Zhenyu Ye, Zhe Tan, Lei Zhou, Debin Gao, Yaohua Wang, Zhenyu Ning, Yupeng Hu

title: High-Performance and Cache-Efficiency Adaptive Radix Tree for Disaggregated Memory
content: Disaggregated memory (DM) architectures enhance resource utilization and architectural scalability by separating computing and memory resources into distinct pools connected via high-speed interconnects, such as RDMA and CXL. Adaptive radix tree (ART) is a widely used range index known for its efficient support of variable-sized keys. However, traditional ART structures incur substantial network overhead in DM architectures during index traversal. In this paper, we propose Sphinx, a high-performance and cache-efficient ART for DM architectures. To minimize network roundtrips during index traversal, Sphinx employs Flat Inner Node Table to eliminate data dependencies among hierarchical ART nodes, enabling memory-level parallelism. Moreover, Sphinx introduces Succinct Filter Cache, which leverages a space-efficient cuckoo filter in the local cache of compute nodes to mitigate read amplification during index traversal. By further incorporating Semi Lock-free ART Nodes, Sphinx achieves high scalability with strong consistency guarantees. Experimental results show that Sphinx outperforms state-of-the-art counterparts by up to 7.3$\boldsymbol{\times}$× in the YCSB benchmark.
author: Bowen Zhang, Shengan Zheng, Jingxiang Li, Shi Shu, Zhenlin Qi, Linpeng Huang, Hong Mei

title: SIFMap: Parallel CNN Inference Using Sub-Input-Feature Maps in PIM
content: Processing-in-memory (PIM) accelerators perform in-situ dot-product operations between input feature maps (IFMs) and convolutional neural network (CNN) weights to accelerate inference. The efficiency of these computations is heavily influenced by the weight mapping strategy. However, existing approaches often adopt IFM-oriented mapping schemes that provide limited parallelism, leading to high latency and low energy efficiency. To address this issue, we propose SIFMap, a subIFM-oriented weight mapping framework designed to enable highly parallel CNN inference. SIFMap leverages the observation that different regions within an IFM contribute unevenly to computation. It first partitions the IFM into fine-grained sub-maps, or subIFMs, based on their computational characteristics. Then, it applies a reinforcement learning (RL) technique to determine optimal weight mapping strategies tailored to each subIFM, optimizing global performance. Furthermore, SIFMap introduces a subIFM-oriented resource allocation scheme to further boost computational parallelism across subIFMs. Experimental results show that SIFMap reduces inference latency by $\mathbf{4.8}{\boldsymbol{\times}}$4.8× and improves energy efficiency by $\mathbf{5.2}{\boldsymbol{\times}}$5.2× compared to state-of-the-art mapping methods under equivalent resource constraints.
author: Tong Wu, Shuibing He, Weijian Chen, Xuechen Zhang, Tuo Shi

title: Trusted Runtime Customizable TEE on FPGA-SoC with User-Controllable TPM
content: To facilitate widespread deployment of FPGA-SoC (Field Programmable Gate Array System-on-Chip) TEE (Trusted Execution Environments) in public clouds, this study proposes TRCTEE, a Trusted Runtime-Customizable TEE approach. TRCTEE incorporates a user-controllable Trusted Platform Module (TPM) which is decoupled from FPGA-SoC and implemented in secure and trusted node, providing both a security-enhanced TEE and a TPM 2.0-supported method for runtime customization for FPGA-SoCs. The principal contributions encompass: (i) Propose a novel FPGA-SoC-CtrlTPM architecture delivering full TPM 2.0 operations for FPGA-SoC TEE; (ii) Enhance security of FPGA-SoC TEE by exploring the trusted boot scheme, TEE-dedicated TPM service, and dynamically measure, deploy, and invoke users’ IPs (Intellectual Properties); (iii) Extend standard TPM command set to support FPGA-SoC-specific security operations. We present a functional prototype implemented on the Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC platform, accompanied by security analysis and performance benchmarking. Experimental results demonstrate TRCTEE’s practical feasibility and enhanced security properties.
author: Jingkai Mao, Junchao Fan, Bocheng Ju, Yanwei Gong, Lin Li, Xiaolin Chang

title: Adaptive Management With Learning-Based Page-Level FTL for Flash-Based SSDs
content: We present LearnedFTL+, a demand-based, page-level flash translation layer (FTL) that integrates learned-index-based translation with adaptive DRAM co-management to improve address translation efficiency in flash-based SSDs. LearnedFTL+ combines two complementary components under a fixed DRAM budget: A cached mapping table (CMT) for locality-rich accesses and a learned-index region for accesses where the CMT becomes ineffective. To make learned indexing practical for SSD address translation, we introduce three key techniques. First, an in-place-update linear model with a bitmap filter ensures that only trustworthy predictions are used for direct translation. Second, a virtual PPN (VPPN) representation constructs contiguous LPN-to-VPPN mappings without restricting physical placement. Third, group-based allocation, together with training assisted by sequential writes and GC, reduces model-training overhead. In addition, LearnedFTL+ supports eviction-driven model initialization and unified eviction across CMT entries and model segments, enabling adaptive DRAM co-management according to runtime access behavior. Experiments on a FEMU-based SSD prototype show that LearnedFTL+ improves throughput by up to 71.6% and reduces I/O latency by 11.9% on average, compared to state-of-the-art page-level FTLs.
author: Haodong Lin, Shengzhe Wang, Zihang Lin, Suzhen Wu, Hong Jiang, Jie Zhang, Yinhui Yu, Bo Mao

title: Secure Hardware Accelerator for Resilience Against Adversarial Attacks in ViTs
content: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated exceptional performance across various computer vision tasks. However, their susceptibility to adversarial white-box attacks poses a significant risk, especially in safety-critical applications. These attacks, with full model access, pose severe threat by drastically reducing accuracy. In response, we propose SAMURAI, a lightweight, preprocessing-based defense pipeline that mitigates adversarial perturbations without requiring model retraining or architectural changes. SAMURAI defends against adversarial inputs by applying a fixed sequence of four transformations: JPEG compression, resizing and center cropping, Gaussian smoothing, and normalization. This process disrupts adversarial attacks while preserving the semantic integrity of the image. Unlike computationally expensive defenses, SAMURAI introduces minimal overhead (e.g., 0.001x for ViT-Large), making it extremely lightweight for real-time deployment. Furthermore, our method generalizes effectively to other vision architectures, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), demonstrating strong transferability. To support efficient deployment in resource-constrained environments, we also design a custom hardware accelerator for the SAMURAI pipeline that enables in-situ preprocessing within accelerators, effectively mitigating adversarial attacks. Experimental results show that SAMURAI achieves robust accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art while requiring only 0.009x the computational cost.
author: Deepraj Majumdar, Anadi Goyal, Sparsh Mittal, Shirshendu Das, Palash Das

title: SSpMV: A Sparsity-Aware Framework for Adaptive Sparse Matrix–Vector Multiplication
content: Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication (SpMV) is a fundamental sparse kernel in both scientific computing and artificial intelligence. However, the performance of existing SpMV algorithms is highly sensitive to diverse sparsity patterns, necessitating an adaptive framework that can effectively extract matrix structures and predict optimal configurations. In this work, we first analyze the performance of parallel SpMV algorithms in various formats. Based on the analysis, we propose Sparsity-aware SpMV (SSpMV), a framework that integrates handcrafted expert features with multimodal representations to automatically determine the optimal algorithm and parameters. At its core is MM-Adapter, a novel multimodal convolutional neural network designed for this selection task. The robustness of SSpMV is validated using a diverse dataset, consisting of nearly the entire SuiteSparse Collection supplemented by finite element matrices. On an Intel Xeon 5120 CPU, SSpMV achieves a selection accuracy of $81.05\%$81.05% and a geometric speedup of $1.26{\boldsymbol{\times}}$1.26× over the MKL spblas IE. Furthermore, on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, it yields $74.12\%$74.12% accuracy and a $1.31{\boldsymbol{\times}}$1.31× speedup over the cuSPARSE baseline.
author: Guoqing Xiao, Shijie Zhao, Qin Du, Shengle Lin, Yuedan Chen, Wangdong Yang, Kenli Li

title: CgDiff: A Context-Based Global Value Predictor With Tagged Geometric History Lengths
content: Value Prediction is a long-standing technique to boost instruction-level parallelism by speculatively breaking data dependencies through predicting register-write values. Existing state-of-the-art predictors, such as EVES, combine computational and context-based approaches but still rely exclusively on local value history, limiting their ability to capture broader correlations. Global value prediction, which exploits correlations across multiple dynamic instructions, has been explored only sparingly. The gDiff predictor first demonstrated the potential of global stride correlations, and EgDiff recently improved upon it with practical refinements. However, both remain PC-localized and thus fail to exploit per-path correlations, where global correlations vary across execution paths. In this work, we propose CgDiff, the first context-based global value predictor. CgDiff augments stride-based global prediction with control-flow history to capture path-sensitive global correlations that elude existing designs. Our evaluation shows that a compact 8.92KB CgDiff not only surpasses a much larger 44KB EgDiff, but also outperforms the state-of-the-art EVES predictor in IPC speedup. Furthermore, a storage-efficient 16.92KB hybrid (CgDiff + EVES) achieves the highest performance among all predictors under comparable budgets. These results demonstrate that context-based global value prediction is a powerful and storage-efficient complement to existing local designs, opening a promising new direction for future research in value prediction.
author: Ling Yang, Libo Huang, Junhui Wang, Zheng Zhong, Yongwen Wang, Li Shen, Wei Chen, Weixia Xu

title: MDN-VJEPA: Multimodal Probabilistic Joint-Embedding World Models
content:
arXiv:2610.13956v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn world models by predicting future representations rather than reconstructing observations. Variational JEPA (VJEPA) gives this prediction probabilistic semantics and permits flexible conditional predictive families. We propose MDN-VJEPA, a multimodal probabilistic JEPA that instantiates the latent predictor as a mixture density network (MDN), representing future states with a Gaussian mixture whose components encode alternative futures, their probabilities, and within-mode uncertainty. For sequential prediction, we address two additional structural requirements: multi-modal futures should remain temporally coherent across a trajectory, and predictive beliefs should remain consistent when propagated to the same horizon through different temporal path compositions, as motivated by the Chapman--Kolmogorov equation. Together, these considerations define a three-level hierarchy of multimodal prediction, coherent multimodal trajectories, and compositionally consistent multimodal dynamics. Controlled experiments show that MDN-VJEPA closely recovers known branching predictive laws, that retaining the complete multimodal belief rather than its conditional mean can lead to materially different and substantially better planning decisions under branching futures, and that trajectory-level coupling and distributional consistency improve temporal coherence and multi-horizon agreement. These results support a simple principle: a probabilistic JEPA should preserve not only how uncertain the future is, but which distinct futures constitute that uncertainty, how they form coherent trajectories, and how those beliefs compose through time.
author: Yongchao Huang

title: LACRM: LLM-Guided Mining of Directed Advertiser Competition Relationships in E-Commerce Advertising
content:
arXiv:2610.13959v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In e-commerce advertising, ad platforms typically fail to model the externalities among advertisers when making optimization decisions: an advertiser's actual performance is largely shaped by rivals competing for the same users; these rivals typically operate in overlapping product categories and at comparable budget scales. However, capturing this rivalry as an explicit, reusable signal is challenging because it is directed, multi-faceted, and partially observable. Existing paradigms such as interaction graphs, taxonomy rules, and single-embedding models do not fully capture these properties. In this paper, we propose LACRM (LLM-driven Advertiser Competition Relationship Mining), a novel framework that constructs directed competition graphs with continuous edge intensities via a three-stage pipeline. LACRM moves beyond symmetric similarity through LLM-driven role-separated profiling, which enables asymmetric multi-route retrieval to uncover both realized and latent rivals. The framework further incorporates listwise learning-to-rank aligned with temporal auction behavior to accurately model directed competition intensity. In offline retrieval experiments on an industrial benchmark, LACRM outperforms strong directed GNN baselines and ablation variants. Multi-LLM and human studies provide complementary evidence that the recovered latent rivals reflect meaningful market competition rather than merely model-generated artifacts. In production A/B tests, LACRM-guided bidding and incentive allocation increase advertising revenue by 1.73% and 1.14%, respectively. The results demonstrate the practical value of explicit competition modeling in large-scale advertising systems.
author: Xiang Shi, Yitian Kou, Bing Li, Shengsheng Niu, Chun Gan, Linghui Meng, Jie He, Zhangang Lin, Ching Law

title: MRFlow: Mechanism-Structured Residual Flow Matching for Virtual Cell Perturbation Prediction
content:
arXiv:2610.13966v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predicting cellular responses to chemical and genetic perturbations is a central test for AI virtual cells, yet many single-cell models reduce each condition to an average expression shift. This target is misaligned with perturbation biology: rare states, resistant subpopulations, and context-dependent effect sizes may coexist under the same intervention. MRFlow treats virtual-cell prediction as conditional transport between empirical single-cell measures. Control and perturbed cells are embedded in a variational latent state space, greedy low-cost supervision is constructed over detached minibatch states, and a conditional flow-matching vector field transports control populations toward perturbed populations. The field decomposes into a mechanism-structured affine dictionary, which recombines shared latent response operators with a low-rank condition-specific correction, and a spectrally controlled residual field for nonlinear cell-level variation. Genetic perturbations are encoded through a regulatory-graph GCN, chemical perturbations through Morgan fingerprints, and both enter the same conditional dynamics interface. Across eight gene and drug perturbation benchmarks, MRFlow attains the highest composite score while preserving competitive raw performance on differential-expression and distributional metrics. The results support latent distribution transport as a principled and empirically effective formulation for perturbation-aware virtual cell modeling.
author: Haojie Yang, Ran Su

title: PRIME: Frequency-Aware Unified Pruning and Merging for MoE Compression
content:
arXiv:2610.13982v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.
author: Shanfeng Huang, Rongqian Zhang, Zhou Fang, Song Xiao, Hai Du

title: DoSA: Dots Sparse Attention
content:
arXiv:2610.13990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. We introduce DoSA (Dots Sparse Attention), a lossless method for making this computation conditional while preserving exact token selection. Its central observation is that Top-K selection requires sufficient evidence to reject a candidate, not necessarily its full score. A seed set supplies a lower bound on the winning threshold. Nonnegative head projections and joint residual bounds upper-bound positive contributions, while activation-informed aggregation bounds the magnitude subtracted by negative heads. The certificate directs full scoring toward candidates that remain eligible; exact-score filtering further reduces writeback and selection work. We establish the certificate and its exact-selection conditions, and analyze how geometry and selection margins govern its effectiveness. Our GPU implementation accelerates the complete Indexer by up to 2.74 times over SGLang and 1.69 times over LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads. End-to-end evaluation on GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves up to 1.94 times and 1.50 times time-to-first-token speedups over the two baselines, respectively.
author: Fanxu Meng, Taosong Fang

title: Predict Before You Modify: Learning Improvement Dynamics for Self-Evolving Agents
content:
arXiv:2610.13991v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. We introduce predictive self-evolution through an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM). Before evaluation, the IDM predicts task-level outcomes of a proposed modification and guides an optional revision. After evaluation, past modifications and their observed outcomes are used to improve the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations. The system can thus improve how it solves tasks, proposes modifications, and predicts their effects. Building on HyperAgents, we evaluate this approach across multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level mathematical grading. Our approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with up to 46% higher average performance over generations. Gains also persist under matched token budgets that include both agent evolution and task evaluation, and extend to held-out tasks. Forecast accuracy improves as the IDM evolves, and the learned predictive knowledge transfers to improve evolution in a new domain.
author: Zixuan Xie, Chang Xu, Yuhua Jiang, Li Zhao

title: Posterior Flow Matching
content:
arXiv:2610.13994v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow matching learns how to transport noise toward data, but its mean prediction does not directly report the endpoint uncertainty remaining at an intermediate state. This paper introduces Posterior Flow Matching (PFM), a general generative modeling framework that learns conditional velocity means and componentwise variances with a Gaussian posterior model. The same model evaluation supplies both a transport prediction and endpoint uncertainty, making posterior diagnostics available throughout generation. These learned moments support a mean-driven ordinary differential equation (ODE) and a posterior-driven stochastic differential equation (SDE), whose local noise scales adapt to the predicted uncertainty. Across image, point-cloud, molecular, and action generation, PFM improves generation quality and provides endpoint-posterior readouts throughout generation.
author: Chenrui Ma, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Xinru Jiang, Tianyang Wang, Yanning Shen, Ferdinando Fioretto

title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
content:
arXiv:2610.13995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.
author: Weixian Waylon Li, Jiaxin Zhang, Han Zhou, Chengzu Li, Ke Wang, Fengxiang He, Yiwen Guo

title: Splicing Hints into Reasoning Traces: Learning from Demonstrator Failures
content:
arXiv:2610.13996v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.
author: Hamed Mahdavi (Pennsylvania State University), Pouria Mahdavinia (Pennsylvania State University), Majid Farhadi (Google), Vasant Honavar (Pennsylvania State University)

title: Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis
content:
arXiv:2610.13998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. The system extracts sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from financial news and incorporates them into a PPO-based trading agent. Experiments on intraday NSE data demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns compared to price-only baselines.
author: Vedanth Padmaraman, Shreen Anand, Vamshi Vishruth J, Vineet V Pai, Arvind Srinath K. T, Subramanyam Natarajan, Shylaja S S

title: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions
content:
arXiv:2610.13999v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.
author: Jincheng Gao, Wei Ding, Shuo Sun

title: VH-GPO: Verified Handoff for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
content:
arXiv:2610.14000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Group-relative reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO train large language model (LLM) agents by comparing rollouts for the same task. When every trajectory in a group fails with the same reward, relative advantages collapse toward zero, leaving no useful learning signal. A frozen teacher can recover from a student-visited state, but letting it complete the task makes the recovered suffix entirely teacher-generated. We ask: after repairing a student failure, when should control return to the student? We propose outcome-verified teacher-student handoff, instantiated in Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). The teacher provides enough support to reach a state from which the student can succeed, then returns control so that successful experience is again student-generated. Given an environment-verified teacher recovery, VH-GPO selects the earliest independently confirmed handoff point found within a bounded search budget. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, VH-GPO increases success rates over GRPO from 59.38% to 94.79% on ALFWorld and from 71.62% to 77.34% on WebShop. Improvements also hold with the 7B student, for which additional teacher and student output tokens amount to 1.77% and 2.61% of regular student rollout output tokens on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the key components. These results support using verified teacher assistance to repair failures while reinforcing the student's ability to complete tasks independently.
author: Haoze Li, Peng Zhou, Peiyuan Wu, Weijie Zhao, Yinan Xin

title: PreSO: Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation
content:
arXiv:2610.14001v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses a self-teacher conditioned on privileged information to turn the sparse outcome signal of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) into dense token-level supervision. Yet the teacher's advantage may depend on information unavailable to the student at inference, raising a central question: which privileged changes are worth distilling? We use cross-problem recurrence as an empirical cue for potentially reusable guidance. Comparing the representation shifts induced by full solutions and compact hints, we find that hint-induced shifts are more concentrated and directionally consistent across problems, and yield more sustained downstream gains despite revealing less information. Motivated by this association, we propose Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation (PreSO). At the source, PreSO uses compact hints to limit the solution-specific detail entering the privileged shift. At the target, it estimates a leading low-rank subspace from shifts pooled across related problems, projects the privilege-induced correction onto this subspace, and adds it to the student's unprivileged representation to form the representation-level distillation target. The selected subspace serves as an operational proxy for recurring structure, rather than a guaranteed separation of transferable and instance-specific information. On five competition-level mathematics benchmarks, PreSO consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, improving average accuracy over the base model by 6.8, 9.0, and 10.0 points. Beyond peak accuracy, PreSO attains the highest final-checkpoint average at every model scale, with improvements that persist through the end of training.
author: Yuhang Yang, Mingxuan Xia, Chao Ye, Shuai Zhu, Shouqing Yang, Haobo Wang, Shenzhi Yang, Zhengqing Zang, Chenglong Wang

title: Showing versus Doing: Teaching by Demonstration
content:
arXiv:2610.14004v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.
author: Mark K. Ho, Michael L. Littman, James MacGlashan, Fiery Cushman, Joseph L. Austerweil

title: Coding LLMs Can Be Harnessed to Learn Interpretable Models from Data
content:
arXiv:2610.14006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Since compact, interpretable classifiers correspond to simple programs, it is natural to ask if LLM-based coding agents can be used to learn interpretable models from data. In this paper we present a simple harness that repeatedly prompts a coding LLM to produce the next rule in a rule set, given a sample of labeled examples. We show that this approach is competitive with, and often superior to, state-of-the-art rule-learning methods on tabular data, especially with small training sets, and wins by large margins on text, including against another LLM-based rule learner; that this approach outperforms standard harnesses, and that the approach immediately leads to new kinds of interpretable models, since coding agents are not restricted to search a highly restricted hypothesis space. In addition to the advances made in learning interpretable models, these results are of interest because they introduce a new class of coding benchmarks - construction of interpretable classifiers - which includes quantitative measurements of output quality (i.e., test-set error) and existing mature ``specialist coding algorithms'' (i.e., existing learning methods).
author: Aditya Kumar, Cassandra A. Cohen, William W. Cohen

title: What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction? Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal
content:
arXiv:2610.14007v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory, universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so ``closer'' can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes certify even that: finite evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot see the constants that carry Solomonoff's guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of predictive success, so Solomonoff's predictor, which leaves part of it unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where it spends it; on mutually singular families this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper.
author: Luan Ozelim, Abicumaran Uthamacumaran, Hector Zenil

title: Generalized PINN-Based Inverse Estimation of Spatially Varying Heat Transfer Coefficients with Transfer Learning
content:
arXiv:2610.14008v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study investigates generalized boundary representations and transfer learning for physics-informed neural-network (PINN) estimation of spatially varying convective heat transfer coefficients (HTCs) in jet impingement cooling. Piecewise-linear (PWL) and neural-network boundary estimators are inferred from transient interior-temperature measurements and evaluated against CFD-CHT reference HTC profiles at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000 and 15000. A discrete Adjoint-FEM formulation with gradient regularization based on the $H^1$-seminorm provides an independent inverse-method comparison. Transfer learning is investigated under two source-target conditions: transfer between noise levels at the same Reynolds number, and transfer from a controlled Gaussian-profile problem to CFD-CHT-derived target problems at different Reynolds numbers. For the representative Re = 5000 target with 5% measurement noise, quadratic, PWL, and neural-network PINNs achieve relative HTC-profile errors of 5.08, 5.31 and 5.19%, respectively, while generalized representations reduce the error for the Re = 15000 target from 16.76% for the quadratic PINN to 14.41% and 14.46%. Transfer learning reduces target-training time by 57.86-81.71% for fixed-Reynolds-number transfer and by 50.59-84.94% for Gaussian-to-CHT transfer. Its effect on reconstruction accuracy is target dependent: fixed-profile PWL transfer remains within 0.30 percentage points of scratch training, whereas Gaussian-to-CHT transfer produces differences of 0.10-1.52 percentage points across targets and representations. These results demonstrate that generalized PINN representations can accommodate spatially varying HTC profiles without a prescribed quadratic form, while transfer learning can substantially reduce target-training cost for repeated inverse estimation, with the resulting reconstruction accuracy depending on source-target compatibility.
author: Pradipan Maitra, Jariful Hassan, Arijit Hazra

title: When Log Parsing Removes What Matters: Detecting Failures in Distributed GPU Workloads
content:
arXiv:2610.14009v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large AI models increasingly rely on distributed GPU execution, yet it remains unclear whether established failure analysis methods transfer effectively to this setting. We introduce GF-Bench, a PyTorch-based framework and dataset for generating diverse failures in distributed GPU workloads. The framework supports extensible workload and fault-injection logic; based on this design, the current release targets failures visible in multi-GPU communication logs and provides 220 labeled two-GPU executions covering normal runs, CUDA out-of-memory fail-stop failures, and persistent straggler fail-slow failures. Using GF-Bench, we evaluate three sequence-based methods (DeepLog, LogAnomaly, and LogBERT) and the LLM-based LogPrompt on parsed logs, and additionally evaluate LogPrompt on raw logs. On parsed inputs, no method reliably detects both failure classes, and the highest overall F1 score is 0.667. Raw inputs raise the overall F1 score of in-context LogPrompt to 0.983, at 9.0x its average input-token usage and 8.7x its per-run cost. These results expose a substantial trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency: generic log parsing lowers operational cost but discards the distributed execution context required for accurate failure detection. GF-Bench provides a reproducible basis for studying cost-efficient analysis methods and can be extended to additional GPU workloads and failure types.
author: Boyuan Cui, Yuyang Zeng, Yifang Tian, Hans-Arno Jacobsen

title: SIRNET: Causal Adaptation of Pretrained Embeddings for Semiparametric Treatment-Effect Estimation Under Surrogacy
content:
arXiv:2610.14011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern experiments increasingly produce rich post-treatment objects---such as text, images, and video---that may provide early surrogate signals for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for a subset of participants. A pretrained encoder can turn such an object into a strong generic embedding, but the embedding is not trained for the estimation tasks required by a causal estimator and may emphasize information irrelevant to the causal target. We propose SIRNET, a Surrogate-Informed Representation adaptation framework for neural-NETwork-based causal estimation in the presence of unstructured post-treatment surrogates. Starting from pretrained surrogate embeddings, SIRNET learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, beyond the generic pretraining objective. The resulting covariate and surrogate representations provide a common interface for these nuisance tasks. The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval are obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. We also validate SIRNET's performance in synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.
author: Lei Shi, Qiuran Lyu

title: Perfect Reconstruction Cannot Show Whether Two Codebooks on a VAE's Latent Space Agree
content:
arXiv:2610.14012v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many systems read the latent space of a variational autoencoder (VAE) as discrete codes, and rely on each latent being read back as the code it was written as. Shannon (1948) took such a shared codebook as given; inside a VAE nothing enforces it. We prove that no item of a standard training report can reveal whether the written and read codes agree on encoded data. We construct two VAEs that reconstruct every input perfectly, infer exactly, and match on every per-example ELBO and every code histogram, yet agreement is one in the first and zero in the second. We then show that the ELBO's own terms bound how far a measured agreement can move: the variational gap bounds the shift to exact inference, and the rate bounds the shift to generation from the prior. For Gaussian posteriors, a mean-field encoder pays an exact price in the gap that depends on its choice of axes. On probabilistic PCA the gap certifies a trained encoder in all 75 settings we test, at agreement between 0.76 and 0.97. On 240 trained VAEs, a floor set by the rate and the dataset size rules out rate-side certification in advance for 66 models, and none of them certifies. The results yield a simple protocol, Certify-or-Measure, for any pipeline that reads a VAE as codes.
author: Yusuke Hayashi

title: Physics-Informed State Space Models for Day-Ahead Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
content:
arXiv:2610.14014v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting requires both strong temporal modeling and adherence to physical PV system constraints. Purely data-driven models often ignore the underlying PV conversion process and may produce predictions that are outside the operational range of a PV system. In this paper, we propose a physics-informed state space framework that combines a differentiable PV conversion model with a selective state space backbone (PowerMamba). Our approach follows a physics-residual decomposition. The physics module provides a structured baseline based on solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits, while the state space model learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. Experiments on one year of utility-scale PV data show that the proposed method significantly improves forecasting accuracy, reducing RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% compared to a physics-only baseline, and outperforming a purely data-driven model. Results further show that incorporating system-level physics provides the largest performance gains, while additional refinements offer only marginal improvements. Beyond accuracy, the model improves robustness by constraining predictions toward physical feasibility, reducing unrealistic predictions under corrupted measurements.
author: Phil Aupke, Muhammad Hassan, Khalid Ali,  Seema, Andreas Kassler, Andreas Theocharis

title: DShuttleNet: A Badminton Doubles Dataset for Evaluating Team Coordination
content:
arXiv:2610.14016v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Most existing sports datasets are individual-centric or ball-centric, focusing on individual player actions while ignoring interactions among teammates. In badminton doubles, tactical success is governed by rapid team formation and coordination, yet standard resources for modeling these player interactions are scarce. To bridge this gap, we present DShuttleNet, a comprehensive dataset for badminton doubles curated from elite BWF World Tour tournaments. Beyond trajectory data, DShuttleNet uniquely incorporates expert-labeled "Loss Reasons," transforming the dataset into a diagnostic tool for causal tactical evaluation. We formally define two geometry-driven representations, Teammate-Relative Angle (TRA) and Vertical Shot Angle (VSA), to characterize coordination and shot aggressiveness. To quantify interpersonal synergy, we introduce novel metrics, Court Coverage Efficacy Index (CCEI) and Threat Load Asymmetry Index (TLAI), which evaluate the often-overlooked non-hitting partner's role and defensive coordination. Experimental results demonstrate that conventional models suffer from underfitting when failing to incorporate these coordination-centric features, highlighting the critical importance and potential impact of releasing DShuttleNet. Dataset is available at: https://doi.org/10.34740/kaggle/dsv/16097938.
author: Guan-Yi Jhang, Chiencheng Chiang, Wei-Kai Chen, Hui-Ching Yu, Hsu-Chao Lai, Hwai-Jung Hsu, Wang Chih-Chuan, Jhy-Cheng Huang, Jiun-Long Huang

title: Barycentric Anchored Weight Search for Robust Model Merging
content:
arXiv:2610.14017v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose Barycentric Anchored Search, a post-hoc weight-space procedure for improving fine-tuned vision models under distribution shift without additional gradient training or increased inference cost. Given a pre-trained initialization and two checkpoints fine-tuned on a source dataset, the method constructs barycentric candidate weights and performs a small derivative-free search along directions connecting each candidate to the pre-trained model. Candidate weights are selected using a small validation subset of one or more out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets; the selected model is then evaluated on the held-out portions of those datasets, on additional OOD benchmarks, and on the ImageNet validation set to quantify the robustness-accuracy trade-off. The method is inspired by simplex-based derivative-free optimization, including Nelder-Mead and Torczon multidirectional search, but is specialized to the geometry of neural network weight merging. Unlike Model Soup, which typically benefits from many fine-tuned checkpoints, and unlike Model Stock, which applies a fixed geometric merge, our approach uses only two fine-tuned checkpoints and iteratively adapts the merge using validation feedback from OOD data. Experiments with CLIP ViT-B/32 show that the proposed search substantially improves performance on held-out OOD data, including ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Sketch, while keeping ImageNet accuracy competitive. The resulting weights also improve transfer to OOD datasets not used during candidate selection, outperforming the original fine-tuned checkpoints, naive model soups, and Model Stock in our evaluations. These results suggest that lightweight optimization in anchored weight space provides a practical alternative to fixed weight-averaging rules, geometric merging, or single-model selection.
author: Antoni Buades, Jose-Luis Lisani

title: CoEvoke: Evoking Multi-Agent Collaboration for Trajectory Collection
content:
arXiv:2610.14021v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training multi-agent collaboration requires trajectories of checking, feedback, and repair, yet task-solving rollouts may end in immediate approval or repeat unsuccessful attempts without useful correction. We introduce CoEvoke, a cross-domain framework that evokes these interactions during trajectory collection. Controlled perturbations create recoverable difficulties, while restricted reference-based guidance directs investigation. The resulting dataset contains 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, linking public interactions to evidence, decisions, and task-native outcomes. Separate experiments over 2,287 same-task pairs show feedback increases of 47.72-100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups; guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training improves ACPBench-Hard success from 35.38% to 42.12% (+6.73 points). SWE verifier training gains 7.60-9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references. Workflow and post-training evaluations preserve task-solving topology with unperturbed inputs and no private-reference guidance. These results support designing collection conditions to obtain corrective supervision that improves collaborative decisions with frozen solving agents.
author: Lin Wu, Shu Yao, Yuheng Wang, Jingru Fan, Huatao Li, Yihan Li, Liu Yixuan, Cheng Liu, Jian Chang, Zeyu Zhao, Aohua Zhang, Huiying Zhao, Shuyuan Zhu, Chen Qian

title: OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision
content:
arXiv:2610.14022v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream computation, then it internalizes these states from on-policy trajectories. OPMD achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher--student settings, and generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that mechanism supervision yields more effective reasoning and meaningfully alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies, supporting that it transfers information beyond output supervision alone. Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.
author: Yingdong Shi, Zhihong Li, Changming Li, Jingyi Yu, Quan Li, Kan Ren

title: Historical Anchors for Scientific Forecasting on Human-Aware Knowledge Graphs
content:
arXiv:2610.14023v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predicting which scientific connections will form next can point researchers toward the most promising leads. One successful approach learns representations by sampling paths through publication networks, represented by a hypergraph, that connect scientific entities, concepts, and researchers, approximating how knowledge and expertise move through the literature. Sampled paths are then used to train an embedding model to forecast scientific connections such as a property of a material. Performance, however, depends strongly on how many paths are sampled: too little sampling yields incomplete representations, while further sampling can eventually weaken prediction quality. The best sampling budget is therefore often identifiable only after future discoveries are known. We introduce Query--Anchor Agreement (QAA), a diagnostic requiring no future labels or separately trained model. QAA can be used to select a sampling budget, and refine or re-rank the resulting forecast to improve forecasting scientific connections. QAA compares the candidates a model predicts for a target with those most similar to the target's known historical examples, and identifies when these two views converge. Across thermoelectric-material and COVID-19 drug-repurposing benchmarks, repeated random-seed runs, and three sampling policies, QAA-selected budgets fall on average 1.86 percentage points below hindsight-optimal selection for broad candidate recovery. Further, promoting candidates supported by both views, under a capped fusion that bounds the anchor contribution, improves broad recovery across all six benchmark-policy settings, which define the types of network walks used for sampling.
author: Siu Tin Wu, Ryan C. Barron, Phoebe Upton Sanderbeck, Kim {\O}. Rasmussen, George Tompkins, Maksim E. Eren

title: Beyond a Better Score: Long-Horizon Agentic ML Development and Evaluation Protocol for Physics Time Series
content:
arXiv:2610.14024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics time-series data are central to fundamental discoveries involving dark matter, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. Machine learning has shown strong potential to recover weak scientific signals buried in complex noise. Recent LLM-agent systems further automate ML development, but existing approaches are often driven primarily by one or a few numerical scores. In pursuit of a better score, agents may exploit shortcuts, trigger mode collapse, or game the evaluation procedure, producing models that achieve high scores but are scientifically invalid. We introduce SIDERIUS, an LLM agent system designed to move beyond a better score toward scientifically valid, long-horizon ML development. SIDERIUS combines contract-defined composable capabilities for flexible orchestration and human-in-the-loop, a multi-layer scientific evaluation protocol that distinguishes valid models from unhealthy or gaming models, and resource-aware exploration for computationally expensive scientific ML. In our TIDMAD benchmark, SIDERIUS with a GPT-based orchestrator achieves the highest Valid-model proposal rate of 63.8% and the best valid denoising score of 2.744, compared with 1.6% and -0.647, respectively, for the same GPT model using the general-purpose Codex coding agent. We further benchmark SIDERIUS on three additional physics time-series datasets, demonstrating its reuse and performance across different tasks. Together, these results suggest that progress in agentic scientific ML should be measured beyond a better score, by how an agent explores and by whether the models it produces can be trusted as science.
author: Yue Ma, Lucas Venetoulias, Akbota Assan, Aobo Li

title: Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering
content:
arXiv:2610.14025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations during inference. For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings.
